newsitem.title: CHINA: China creating state conglomerates, but not smooth.
newsitem.headline: China creating state conglomerates, but not smooth.

text.p: China is forcing many state enterprises to merge into huge conglomerates in the hope of increasing efficiency, but economists said the measure could in some cases just make things worse.
Shanghai is taking the lead to create a series of world-class industrial powerhouses to drag the whole loss-making state sector towards profitability, they said.

China's state-owned enterprises reported a record loss of three billion yuan in the first quarter of 1997, the first such deficit for the sector since the country embarked on its course of economic reform in 1979.

"Theoretically, China is moving in the right direction by forming big holding companies to increase efficiency," said an economist with the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. "But so far the plan has not been running smoothly."
The strategy being followed is to encourage or force profitable state-owned enterprises to take over loss-making firms operating in the same industrial sector.

The larger firm takes over the bankrupt firms' assets and becomes responsible for its staff. The extent to which it also takes on its debts is to some extent negotiable, judging from publicised examples so far.

"Most of mergers are not totally market-oriented," the economist said. "The government plays a big role in these mergers, some are totally arranged by the government. That results in operational difficulties and increased friction in management."

Official media earlier this year reported that Shanghai, China's major industrial centre, plans to set up two or three "super large" enterprises, each with annual sales of 100 billion yuan ($12 billion) by the end of the century.
It also wants to set up another 15 large groups, each with five billion yuan in annual sales and 10 with 10 billion yuan of annual sales each.

"This process of mergers makes sense for some companies, but the basic problem with the state enterprises is marketing and management, and overall mergers don't help at all in that area," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
"If a company itself wants to do mergers and chooses its own takeover targets, it will put business considerations first," said an analyst with a local consultancy company.
"But the big profitable firms are also required to help the government to maintain social stability," he said. "This results in some sacrifices in profits."
That is a sacrifice Beijing insists some healthy state firms make in order to ensure there is no mass lay-off of workers as the bankrupt firms are wound up.
Three years ago, for instance, the Sanqiang textile group in Shanghai had a relatively healthy debt/asset ratio of around 60 percent.
Since then it has taken over seven other firms on the edge of bankruptcy and now has a debt/asset ratio of 90 percent, a company official said.
"The seven companies have brought us 150 million yuan in losses and 350 million yuan in debts," he said. "That's why we have such a high asset/debt ratio."
Several of the mergers announced recently have involved listed firms, and some brokerage analysts say they are unconvinced that the mergers were in the best interests of shareholders.

"If a financial restructuring proposal brings no new source of profit but rather requires shareholders to invest more money, it should be seriously reconsidered," the official China Securities newspaper said last week.
